1. Introduction
Sound is a part of our surroundings arising from the vibrations of objects that travel through gas, liquid, or solid materials. It shapes
our experiences, from the soothing melodies sung by a mother to her child to the rhythmic beats of our favorite songs. However, when
sound becomes unwanted or disruptive, it transforms into noise [1,2]. In our changing environment, noise pollution has grown

exponentially, infiltrating peaceful spaces with its relentless clamor. This intrusion disrupts the tranquility of our surroundings and has
tangible adverse effects on human well-being [3,4]. These effects include increased stress levels, disturbances in sleep patterns,
cognitive impairments, and even cardiovascular issues [5–8]. Recognizing these impacts, a movement exists to address and manage
noise pollution. Various strategies are being implemented to coexist with sound in a noisy world [9]. These strategies encompass
interventions, urban planning initiatives, and policy-making efforts.
Given the growing urgency to tackle noise pollution concerns, the scientific community has devoted efforts to developing and
refining methods for measuring sound absorption [10–12]. Various techniques have been introduced with varying complexity, pre-
cision levels, and specific applications [13,14]. Measurements conducted in real-world environments provide insights into the
behavior of sound, considering factors such as existing structures, atmospheric conditions, and other ambient influences [15,16]. On
the other hand, experimental methods conducted in controlled settings allow for measurements by isolating specific variables, leading
to a deeper understanding of how sound is absorbed. Balancing these two approaches is crucial when developing strategies for
managing noise [17,18].
Considering the impacts of noise pollution, numerous solutions have been conceived, designed, and put into practice. One key
aspect of these initiatives involves using construction materials that possess absorption properties [19–23]. Pervious concrete, with its
structure, proves to be a choice in urban areas where drainage and noise reduction are essential [24–26]. Likewise, integrating ag-
gregates into concrete provides an advantage, reducing structural weight while enhancing sound absorption capabilities [23,27,28].
The advancements in materials and aerated concrete have introduced construction materials that function with effective sound ab-
sorption, thereby reducing disruptive noises [29]. However, evaluating these materials based on their ability to absorb sound and
considering factors like strength, durability, and environmental sustainability is essential.
In the exploration of room settings, room acoustics emerges as a discipline that merges architectural aesthetics with acoustic
functionality. The selection of materials, including panels and diffusers, plays a crucial role in sculpting the auditory experience within
a space. However, the influence extends beyond materials alone; the architectural design and spatial geometry of the room possess the
capability to either amplify or attenuate sound [30,31]. Simultaneously, there has been a resurgence in acoustic simulations driven by
advancements in capabilities. The wave-based approach, in particular, has gained popularity among simulation techniques due to its
precision in modeling intricate sound behaviors across diverse environments. These simulations thoroughly consider source charac-
teristics, room geometry, material properties, and the presence of humans, solidifying their role as essential tools for both design and
research applications [32–35].
While cement-based materials have demonstrated sound absorption properties in their various forms, caution is necessary when
considering their widespread utilization. Challenges related to cost may emerge during the deployment of formulations, potentially
impeding scalability [36,37]. Durability also poses a concern, as certain types of concrete may compromise long-term structural
integrity [22,23]. Furthermore, as environmental concerns gain significance, it is crucial not to overlook the carbon footprint and
ecological impacts associated with the production and disposal of concrete [24]. Therefore, while concrete solutions show promise, it
is essential to undertake evaluations that consider various perspectives.
The literature review commences by shedding light on the complexities of sound and noise through an analysis of existing liter-
ature. The subsequent section clarifies methods for evaluating the sound absorption performance of various materials. Following this,
diverse types of cement-based materials for sound absorption will be discussed, along with an investigation into different frequency
ranges utilized for analysis. Finally, room acoustics and simulation will be addressed.
1.1. Background
The study of acoustics has roots in civilizations, where it played a pivotal role at the intersection of science, art, and architecture.
Noteworthy examples include the ancient Greek theaters such as the Epidaurus theater, renowned for their impeccable design, which
enabled even whispers to be heard by audiences [38,39]. These historical wonders highlight how our ancestors appreciated the nu-
ances of sound, skillfully manipulating them to craft immersive auditory experiences. However, the contemporary understanding of
acoustics transcends historical marvels. It now integrates principles from physics, engineering, and sensory perception. Sound, gov-
erned by the physics of wave propagation and interaction [40], transforms when it encounters different spaces and materials,
significantly influencing our experiences. These interactions extend beyond concert halls or theaters, permeating our homes, work-
places, public spaces, and every aspect of our environment.
In densely populated and built-up areas, diverse acoustic challenges emerge. The crowded cityscape, with its buildings, heavy
traffic, and constant human activity, often magnifies sounds, creating an environment that can be both chaotic to hear and psycho-
logically distressing [5–7]. The evolving landscape of these challenges highlights the significance of acoustics as both an art form,
focusing on aesthetics, and as a crucial science centered around public health and well-being.
Given these multifaceted implications, the study of acoustics has become more critical than ever. Successfully navigating the
modern urban environment requires a profound and comprehensive understanding of how sound behaves and interacts. This
knowledge not only facilitates the development of strategies to mitigate noise pollution but also emphasizes the importance of
designing spaces that enhance overall auditory experiences [41,42].
1.2. Understanding sound and noise perception
Sound, as a physical phenomenon, consists of pressure variations in a elastic medium such as air. These variations, originating from
vibrating objects, propagate as longitudinal waves through the medium [15]. The mechanics of these waves are governed by pa-
rameters such as frequency, which determines the pitch, and amplitude, which affects the perceived loudness [40]. High-frequency
vibrations produce high-pitched sounds, while the amplitude correlates with the energy of the wave, influencing its intensity. In

acoustics, sound is further analyzed through its spectral content, temporal characteristics, and spatial properties. Advanced analytical
techniques allow for the decomposition of sound into its constituent frequencies, facilitating a deeper understanding of complex
auditory scenes [43]. This spectral analysis is crucial for various applications, including noise control, architectural acoustics, and
audio signal processing.
Noise, in contrast to sound, is often defined in psychoacoustic terms as any unwanted or disruptive auditory stimulus [1,2]. The
distinction between sound and noise is inherently subjective and context-dependent. For instance, an urban soundscape might be
perceived as noise pollution by some, while others might find it stimulating or even essential for their daily routine [44,45]. This
subjectivity is influenced by individual auditory perception, psychological factors, and the context in which the sound is experienced.
Quantitative assessment of sound involves measuring its intensity in W/m2, frequently expressed in the decibel (dB) scale, which
provides a logarithmic representation of sound pressure levels [10–12]. Sound level meters and advanced acoustic measurement tools
are employed to capture sound data across different environments, aiding in the identification of noise pollution sources and the
development of mitigation strategies [12].
1.3. Acoustic absorbers
Sound management in various settings, such as recording studios, residences near highways and railways, and lecture halls, relies
on the strategic implementation of acoustic absorbers. These absorbers, carefully designed materials, or structures, aim to diminish
energy by either blocking or reflecting sound waves, converting them into a different form of energy, primarily heat. This trans-
formative capability is crucial for establishing controlled sound environments, ensuring that specific spaces remain free from echoes,
reverberations, or noise pollution [46].
To comprehend the functionality of acoustic absorbers function, an exploration of their interaction with sound waves is imperative.
Whether it is a panel in a studio or a sophisticated baffle in a concert hall, their fundamental purpose remains consistent. As sound
waves encounter these absorbers, their design and material composition effectively minimize reflections. Sound waves scatter in
various directions due to the structure of the absorber or penetrate it, dissipating within its material. This process aims to reduce the
energy of the waves and their impact on the surrounding environment [47].
The sound absorption coefficient, denoted as α, is a dimensionless measure ranging from 0 to 1, indicating the fraction of sound
energy absorbed by a material. An α of 0 means no sound absorption, while an α of 1 indicates total sound absorption. This coefficient is
critical in evaluating the acoustic properties of materials [13]. Professionals in this field rely on measurements in chambers known as
reverberation rooms, equipped with measurement microphones and measurement system to determine this covcbvn efficient. These
controlled environments enable an assessment of how different absorbers respond to frequencies of sound energy [13,14,48–50].
1.4. Contrasting sound behavior
Sound reflection is a fundamental aspect of acoustics, where sound waves bounce back upon encountering obstacles or surfaces [15,
51]. This phenomenon is commonly experienced in environments like canyons, where voices return as echoes. Similarly, in large
rooms with extensive surfaces, echoes can be created due to substantial sound wave reflection. Transmission Loss (TL) is a measure of
the reduction in sound intensity as it passes through a material or structure. It is typically expressed in decibels (dB) and quantifies the
effectiveness of sound insulation materials. For a thorough understanding and proper definition, refer to standard texts and the ISO
10140 series, which outline the methodology for measuring sound insulation in buildings and building elements [52].
In contrast to reflection, absorption refers to how materials consume energy rather than reflecting it. Certain materials can absorb
waves predominantly converting them into heat energy [53]. This property is particularly evident in materials with surfaces like foam
or specialized textiles, commonly used in environments where sound control is essential, such as recording studios or theaters [54]. To
evaluate how effectively these materials absorb sound, we use the absorption coefficient, a metric introduced in Section 1.2. This
coefficient measures the extent to which a material can absorb sound, providing a quantitative basis for assessing acoustic properties.
1.5. Impacts and implications of noise pollution
Noise pollution is a prevalent concern in our contemporary world, characterized by intrusive and overwhelming sounds that
disrupt our daily lives [55]. It encompasses not just random noises, but the unwanted and disruptive auditory experiences caused by
human activities. These disturbances originate from diverse sources reflecting the complexity of modern life, whether it is the hum of
machinery or the chaotic symphony of honking cars during rush hour, each contributing to the growing noise that defines many
cityscapes [56,57].
While noise pollution may initially be perceived as an inconvenience or annoyance, prolonged exposure to chaotic sounds has
profound implications for our well-being. It extends beyond disrupting our peace; it can have significant psychological consequences
[16,58,59]. Disrupted sleep, a crucial process for rejuvenation, can result in more than just tiredness; it can also impact cognitive
function and mood [1,5]. Moreover, prolonged exposure to increased noise levels has been associated with a high risk of diseases,
emphasizing the considerable health risks linked to this problem [60,61].
Addressing the challenges posed by noise pollution requires a comprehensive understanding of its extent. The utilization of noise
metrics is crucial in assessing sound levels. Specifically, the Sound Pressure Level (SPL) is measured in Pa and expressed in dB and is a
logarithmic measure of the effective pressure of a sound relative to a reference value (20 μPa). This is different from the sound intensity
level, which also uses dB but measures the power per unit area (W/m2) [62]. Recognizing the health impact of prolonged noise
exposure, various health organizations and governments have established thresholds. These benchmarks serve as valuable guidelines
for identifying potentially harmful environments and assist policymakers and urban planners in developing strategies to mitigate the
effects of noise pollution [1].

impacts of noise pollution in both urban and rural settings, emphasizing the need for joint international efforts and community-specific
noise management strategies to address the unsustainable increase in environmental noise pollution [64].
2. A comprehensive review of sound absorption measurement techniques
2.1. Introduction
There are various ways and methodologies for measuring the sound absorption of materials, with the American Society for Testing
and Materials (ASTM) and the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) providing detailed test standards. When assessing
the sound absorption of specific materials using these standards, two key aspects must be considered: sound absorption and trans-
mission loss.
These measurement approaches are categorized into the reverberation chamber, impedance tube, and in situ surface impedance
techniques (absorption and reflection method), outlined in detail in the following subsections and summarized in Table 1.
2.2. Reverberation chamber method
The two standards employing the reverberation chamber technique to assess the sound absorption of material are ASTM C423-17
and ISO 354:2019 [13,65]. These methods measure sound absorption by utilizing the concept of reverberation, comparing the
chamber with and without the sample to observe how sound-absorbing materials reduce sound pressure over time. In addition, the
testing approach incorporates sound generated from multiple sources, as depicted in Fig. 1. The diffuse sound field achieved in a
reverberation chamber is inherently different from the complex acoustic environments found in practical applications. The uniform
distribution of sound energy in all directions within a chamber does not replicate the directional sound propagation and varying
absorption characteristics present in real-world settings. Research highlights the significant discrepancies observed in interlaboratory
tests due to factors such as equipment control, source and microphone positions, and room configurations. For instance, Cops et al.
[66] discussed the substantial variances in absorption coefficients measured across different laboratories, attributing them to the
non-ideal diffuseness of the sound field and the physical setup of the measurement environments. Similarly, Müller-Trapet and
Vorl¨ander [67] analyzed the uncertainties in standardized measurements, emphasizing the impact of spatial fluctuations and the
configuration of the test specimen and room on the accuracy of absorption and scattering coefficients, enhancing its credibility.
Furthermore, under the standards, the chamber’s walls are non-parallel to enhance reflectivity and dispersion, while maintaining
uniform pressure. Bischel et al. noted several variances in the parameters employed, although their fundamental principles remain
consistent [17]. These standards differ in parameters such as temperature and humidity, minimum sample size, the number of sound
sources, the number of microphones used, and the reporting method for data.

Although effective, the reverberation method has its limitations. It requires a larger sample size and is sensitive to the sample’s
placement in different testing chambers. This can lead to variability in results, including the possibility of overestimating absorption

evaluate the sound absorption of materials, with variations in parameters such as humidity levels, sample size, number of sound
sources, microphones, and methods of reporting data.
2.3. Impedance tube method
The impedance tube method employs a sound perpendicular to the specimen, in contrast to the reverberation method, which uses a
sound from a different direction. Various standards in this method rely on factors like the number of microphones, types of sound, and
methods for calculating sound absorption. This method adheres to key standards, notably ISO 10534 and ASTM C384 [14,48]. ISO
10534 is divided into parts 1 and 2, and it also includes additional parts that concentrate on variables such as the number and
placement of microphones, along with the analysis method. On the other hand, ASTM C384 is structured as a single part. Other ASTM
standards, including ASTM E1050 and E2611, use the transfer function method as developed by Chung and Blaser in 1980 [48].
While these methods share similarities in their equipment and the use of a reference sample, they can be effectively compared based
on sample size, measurement method, frequency ranges, test setup, and underlying principle. This method typically employs a much
smaller sample size than the reverberation method, and the size depends on the frequency range to be studied [47]. A sample size in the
size of 100 mm is recommended for frequencies up to 1600 Hz, while a sample size of 30 mm or less is recommended for frequencies up
to 6300 Hz. The maximum frequency that can be accurately measured is influenced by the diameter of the sample. Frequencies that
surpass a certain threshold may induce cross modes, which could affect the planarity of the incident and reflected waves, thereby
impacting the precision of the measurements. Equations (2) and (3) are utilized for circular and rectangular samples, respectively, to
perform calculations. The lower limit, on the other hand, relies on both the tube diameter and length, as shown in Equations (2)–(4).

Despite its simplicity and cost-effectiveness, the approach cannot accurately measure non-locally responding materials. In addition,
the method requires core samples to be measured in the tube, which is a distractive method that can alter the sound absorption values

impedance tube method, as detailed in standards like ISO 10534 and ASTM C384, utilizes sound perpendicular to the sample and
varies in terms of microphone number, sound types, and calculation methods. It offers a more precise measurement for smaller samples
compared to the reverberation method, employing both the standing wave and transfer function methods, but it is limited by its
requirement for sample size and potential inaccuracies with non-locally responding materials.
2.3.2. Challenges in converting results
Converting results between these two methods is non-trivial and has been the subject of extensive research. The primary challenge
lies in the fact that the diffuse field method integrates absorption over all angles of incidence, while the normal incidence method
measures absorption at a single angle. This discrepancy can lead to significant differences in the reported absorption coefficients,
especially for materials whose absorption properties vary with the angle of incidence.
Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue, including empirical correlations and theoretical models that account
for the angular dependence of absorption. For instance, London [80] and Olynyk and Northwood [81] have explored methods to
predict diffuse field absorption coefficients from normal incidence measurements by considering factors such as edge diffraction and
finite sample size effects.
2.3.3. Finite-size sample effect
Another important factor to consider is the finite-size sample effect, which can lead to higher absorption coefficients in the diffuse
field method. When a small sample is placed in a large, highly reflective room, diffraction around the edges of the sample can enhance
its apparent absorption. This effect is less pronounced in the normal incidence method, where the sample size relative to the wave-
length of the incident sound wave is a critical parameter. Rindel [82] discussed how the field impedance of a sample can be affected by
its size, suggesting that smaller samples may exhibit higher absorption coefficients due to increased edge diffraction and other
boundary effects. This phenomenon underscores the importance of considering sample size and mounting conditions when inter-
preting absorption measurements and converting between different methods.
In summary, while the diffuse sound field method (ISO 354) and the normal incidence method (ISO 10534-1, (cid:0) 2) provide valuable
insights into the acoustic properties of materials, they are inherently different and can yield disparate results. Researchers and
practitioners must be aware of these differences and the associated challenges in converting measurements between the two methods.
Citing relevant literature and understanding the finite-size sample effect is essential for accurate acoustic characterization and
application.
2.4. In-situ surface impedance method
2.4.1. P-U sensor method
The in-situ surface impedance method represents a significant advancement in measuring material acoustic properties under real-

world conditions. This technique, relatively recent compared to the laboratory methods discussed earlier [83,84], is tailored for field
measurements and employs a P-U probe to determine the material’s impedance, particularly for flat samples. This approach involves
monitoring both the sound pressure (P) and particle velocity (U) using a sensor with dimensions of 3 mm ×1 mm ×0.5 mm, which is
small compared to the wavelength of audible frequencies. The key to this method lies in its ability to accurately capture acoustic
properties in situ, that is, in the material’s actual installation environment. This differs from laboratory methods where the material’s
impedance might be inaccurately represented due to the influence of surrounding materials. The sound pressure in this context is
associated with acoustic potential energy, while the particle velocity relates to acoustic kinetic energy.
One of the notable advantages of the in-situ impedance method is its flexibility in sample size requirements. The test is performed
on a sample that is larger than those used in impedance tube methods, yet considerably smaller than the sample sizes required for
reverberation chamber tests [85]. This enhances its practicality and manageability in various settings. However, it is recommended to
use a sample with a minimum size of 0.065 m2 to ensure reliable measurements [23,25,86,87].
Environmental factors, including temperature fluctuations, wind, and the alignment of the sound intensity probe, can significantly
influence the test outcomes. Therefore, the careful placement of the probe and the speaker is crucial. During the test, the speaker
should be positioned at least 0.26 m away from the sample, and the distance from the sample to the probe should be maintained at
approximately 0.005 m. This spacing is essential to avoid any wave interaction, thereby ensuring the accuracy of the measurements.
Moreover, the method allows for the convenient measurement of both pressure and particle velocity by selecting the type of sound
from the software. From these measurements, the absorption at the sample surface can be calculated, either from the measured
impedance or intensity. When measuring a sample, it is essential to first measure the room without any sample to avoid any reflections
in the air and determine the impedance of the room, using it as a calibration technique. Subsequently, the impedance of the sample is
measured to determine both the sound absorption and the reflection of the sample. In summary, the in-situ impedance method bridges
the gap between the impedance tube and reverberation chamber methods [83–85], offering a more flexible and environment-sensitive
approach to measuring material acoustic properties.
2.4.2. Surface impedance method for reflective properties of noise barriers
The other approach to in-situ measurement involves the use of the impulse response method. This technique focuses on measuring
the reflection component of the impulse response when the measurement equipment is directed toward the barrier with a specific
incidence angle [88–90]. The reflection component is determined by subtracting the free-field impulse response from the measured kth
angle impulse response. This method is outlined in standards like EN 1793-5:2016 [18], which recommend the use of the Maximum
Length Sequence (MLS) signal for these measurements. However, there are suggestions that the Exponential Sine Sweep (ESS) signal
might be a better choice due to its immunity to the system’s nonlinearities and time variance. The use of MLS is generally suitable for
laboratory measurements under controlled conditions, but its outdoor, in-situ application requires careful usage to avoid objects,
especially for segments within a certain time window. This method requires a substantial 4 ×4 m sample area, with nine microphones
set up in a 0.4 m interval rectangular grid. The central microphone is positioned in the middle of the 2 m tall noise barrier. For
standardization, the loudspeaker is placed 1.50 m from the noise barrier’s reference plane, while the measuring grid is located 0.25 m
from this plane [18].
In this method, the analysis involves two distinct nine-channel impulse responses: one captured in front of the noise barrier,
containing both direct and reflected sounds, and the other in a free field, containing only direct sounds. The energy of the sound
reflected off the barrier is determined by contrasting these two impulse responses. Since both responses are measured above the
ground, they include ground reflection components. The response in front of the barrier additionally captures diffraction effects at the
barrier edges. Accurate elimination of unwanted components is achieved by measuring the impulse response at a significant height
above the ground and with a large enough sample, applying the Adrienne time window for precision [77,88].

3. Modified cementitious materials for acoustic absorption
Modified concrete incorporates additional materials with the aim of improving its acoustic properties, specifically enhancing its
sound absorption capabilities. These modifications often involve the integration of lightweight aggregate, hump aggregate, foam
concrete, and aerated concrete. Standard concrete typically exhibits a sound absorption coefficient of approximately 0.02, meaning
that it reflects 98 % of the sound that strikes its surface, thus demonstrating very limited sound absorption capabilities. To provide a
clearer comparison of the sound absorption performance of various types of concrete, Table 2 presents a summary of significant
findings, highlighting the sound absorption coefficients of different concrete materials in comparison to reference samples [19].
3.1. Pervious concrete
Pervious concrete, also known as porous concrete, derives its name from its high porosity and has typically porosity values ranging
from 15 % to 25 % [25], characterized by internal interconnected or separate pores. The key ingredients for producing pervious
concrete include cement, coarse aggregate, and a minimal amount of fine aggregate. Various aggregates, including recycled materials,
vermiculite [73], recycled concrete, and bottom ash [74], can be incorporated, with aggregate sizes ranging from gap-graded to
uniform [101]. A lower water-cement ratio can be employed to enhance strength. While its porosity makes it suitable for sound and
heat absorption, it compromises strength, making it unsuitable for structural applications. However, pervious concrete finds utility as
an insulating material [99,102,105].
Numerous studies have investigated the impact of coarse aggregate size distribution and the nature of the material, be it natural or
recycled, on sound absorption performance. For instance, Kim et al. [20] employed expanded shale as light coarse aggregate with sizes
ranging from 4 to 19 mm, categorized into three parts: 4–8 mm, 8–12 mm, and 12–19 mm. Their findings suggested that altering the
aggregate size does not significantly affect sound absorption, but using smaller sizes creates larger pores due to the higher surface area
of the aggregate, leading to increased micropores on the surface, which, in turn, requires more cement. Conversely, Neithalath et al.
[106] investigated the effect of the natural aggregate size on sound absorption, using sizes of 2.36, 4.75 and 9.50 mm, comparing them
with a single-size aggregate sample. They concluded that incorporating different sizes of aggregates in the matrix enhances pore
effectiveness by increasing porosity, thus improving sound absorption. Therefore, when comparing these studies, it’s evident that
while both identify benefits in modifying aggregate sizes, Kim et al. emphasize the practical considerations of smaller aggregates,
whereas Neithalath et al. highlight the acoustic advantages of a varied size mix in the matrix for optimal sound absorption.
The studies on the replacement ratio and type of aggregate replacement in pervious concrete indicate that a higher preplacement
ratio with lower-density aggregate tends to yield improved sound absorption results. Notably, the use of expanded shale with various
sizes has demonstrated superior sound absorption capabilities in comparison [93,107]. In summary, pervious concrete, renowned for
its high porosity, proves effective in sound absorption but is unsuitable for structural application. The size and type of aggregate,
particularly lightweight options like expanded shale, significantly influence its sound-absorbing properties, with a higher replacement
ratio of lower-density aggregates resulting in enhanced performance.

density of around 2.65 g/cm3. On the other hand, crumb rubber, used as an alternative aggregate material, typically has a specific

aggregates range from 1 to 6 mm. This variation in density and size affects the material’s properties and suitability for different
construction applications. Due to its low specific gravity, resulting samples become low-density, thereby enhancing acoustic

3.3. Foamed (cellular) concrete
Foamed or cellular concrete is a mixture consisting of water, cement, and minimal or no fine aggregate [111], including a certain
percentage of foaming agents contributing to a lower density of concrete. The density of foamed concrete typically ranges from 300 to
1600 kg/m3, depending on the foaming agent dosage. In terms of acoustic performance, Zhang et al. [72,103] discovered that the
foaming agent dosage influences sound absorption with higher dosages leading to improved sound absorption due to increased
porosity and tortuosity within the material matrix. Additionally, Stolz et al. [104] demonstrated that using a higher amount of foaming
agent with fine aggregate can decrease sound absorption because the fine aggregate requires more water, which affects pore formation
and, consequently, sound absorption. In summary, the acoustic performance of foamed concrete, influenced by its foaming agent
dosage, improves sound absorption through increased porosity and tortuosity. However, incorporating fine aggregates into this mix
can diminish sound absorption, as it necessitates more water, thereby impacting pore formation.
3.4. Aerated concrete
Aerated concrete incorporates alumina or other air-entraining agents, with aluminum powder being the most common. The powder
reacts with calcium hydroxide, a cement hydrate, releasing the hydrogen gas and creating the pore inside the matrix. These pores
resulted in a low concrete density ranging from 250 kg/m3 to 1600 kg/m3, with porosity levels between 15 % and 91.5 %, depending
on the amount of dosage used [112]. Sound absorption is enhanced in aerated concrete due to the high connectivity between the pores,
making the sound lose energy effectively. The primary advantage of aerated concrete over foamed concrete lies in its higher number of
open pores, contributing to enhanced sound absorption. In summary, aerated concrete, characterized by its low density and high
porosity due to aluminum-induced pores, offers superior sound absorption through its abundant open pores compared to foamed
concrete.
3.5. Influence of key parameters: density, porosity, and surface area on sound absorption
3.5.1. Density
The study of the relationship between material density and acoustic properties, particularly in sound absorption materials, is a key
focus in acoustical research. High-density materials offer the benefit of increased strength and durability, becoming more robust and
resistant to wear, which is essential in applications demanding long-term reliability [113]. However, these dense materials tend to be
less efficient in absorbing sound. As explained by Anand et al. [114], they can be likened to a mass-spring system, acting more as
barriers that diminish the transmission of low-frequency sounds rather than absorbing them. This understanding is critical in selecting
materials for specific acoustic applications.
However, it is essential to note that there are trade-offs associated with the benefits of high-density materials. One significant
drawback is their reduced effectiveness in absorbing high-frequency sounds. This limitation stems from their low porosity, which
restricts the material’s ability to absorb and dissipate high-frequency sound waves effectively. A characteristic feature of dense sub-
stances [21,108]. When sound waves travel through materials, pores act as channels or cavities that capture and dissipate energy [23].
The scarcity of these channels in high-density materials makes them less effective against high-frequency sounds [22].
Furthermore, practical considerations come into play when evaluating the feasibility of using materials in construction and
acoustic applications. High density inherently adds weight to the materials. While this can be beneficial, it also presents challenges that
may increase transportation and installation costs for absorption purposes. Likewise, the expenses related to materials can increase
when dealing with substances due to their mechanical properties. Therefore, finding the balance between density and operational
sound quality becomes crucial when selecting and designing materials. To achieve this balance, many researchers have used different
materials and methods to reduce the weight as well as to increase the sound absorption performance [20,93,97,98]. Some researchers

3.5.2. Porosity
The presence of holes, known as porosity in materials, significantly influences their interaction with sound, particularly in the
context of noise management [119]. Porous materials are highly effective at absorbing waves at higher frequencies, and this ab-
sorption is mainly dependent on porosity, which in turn affects tortuosity and airflow resistivity as they are directly related. Tortuosity
is defined as the ratio of the actual path length that sound waves travel through a porous material to the direct path length. It measures
the complexity of the paths that sound waves must navigate. High tortuosity means the sound waves travel through more convoluted
paths, increasing their interaction with the material and thus enhancing sound absorption. Airflow resistivity is the resistance
encountered by air as it flows through a material’s pores, measured in Rayls per meter (Pa⋅s/m2). This parameter is crucial in
determining the material’s sound absorption performance. Higher airflow resistivity indicates greater resistance to airflow, which
particularly enhances the absorption of lower-frequency sounds. These factors affect sound absorption because they redirect the en-
ergy of the sound waves, transforming it into other forms, such as heat. A study by Moges et al. [23] explores the intricate relationship
between porosity and sound absorption, explicitly focusing on cement-based materials. The findings of the study further affirm the
performance of substances when handling high-frequency sounds.
In addition to their sound-absorbing characteristics, porous materials offer a range of additional benefits that have been widely
recognized. Their structure, characterized by spaces and openings, naturally provides properties that assist in retaining heat, providing
advantageous in situations where temperature control is essential [120,121]. Additionally, the lightweight nature of porous materials
makes them easier to transport, install, and manage overall structural load, as noted by Mitrevska et al. [122].
However, despite the advantage of porosity, it also poses challenges when extensively utilized. One significant concern relates to
the strength of the material. An overly porous material may lack the stiffness and durability required for structural applications, as
insisted by Kebede et al. [23]. This limitation highlights the need to balance between ensuring sound performance and maintaining the
material’s structural integrity, as discussed by Elrahman et al. [123] and Wu et al. [115]. Moreover, while porosity is inherently
advantageous for absorbing sound waves, it is crucial to design and distribute the pores carefully; however, when using air-entraining,
especially Aluminum powder (Al), the pore distribution is anisotropic, meaning that the use of Al in cement-based materials can induce
a relatively large and anisotropic pore distribution as indicated by Shabbar et al. [124] and Elrahman et al. [123]. Designed or un-
evenly distributed pores can lead to issues such as sound reflection or scattering that can detract from the primary purpose of sound
absorption provided by these materials. This emphasizes the importance of meticulous pore design, as emphasized by Elrahman et al.
[123]. Their observations highlight that although the concept of porosity holds potential, its effectiveness is closely tied to how it is
implemented and executed in the field of acoustics. In summary, porosity in materials improves high-frequency sound absorption due
to their channel structures, but it presents challenges in maintaining strength and requires careful pore design to avoid issues like
sound reflection, emphasizing the need for balance in acoustic applications.
3.5.3. Surface area
When considering how materials behave acoustically, surface area plays a role. The principle is that a larger surface area allows for
more interactions with sound waves, leading to better energy dissipation [125] The long-term performance and sustainability of
construction materials fundamentally rely on their durability. Cementitious materials, are traditionally valued for their robustness in
construction. When the surface is exposed to sound, it has a greater ability to absorb and reduce that sound [22]. Additionally, as
indicated by Neithalath et al. and Kim et al., the main factor contributing to the sound absorption performance of pervious concrete is
that a portion of sound energy can be dissipated as air passes through a large number of pores or apertures [3,92,101,126]. However, it
is not solely about expanding the surface area; the nature and design of surfaces also impact acoustics. Complex geometries with
patterns, cavities, and undulating forms create pathways for sound waves to navigate through. Such intricate designs ensure sound
waves interact with the surface multiple times, enhancing absorption across frequencies [22,127]. In summary, larger surface areas
and complex geometrical designs in materials enhance sound absorption by providing more pathways for sound wave interaction and
energy dissipation.
3.5.4. Optimization of the parameters
In the realm of technology, the intricate relationship between density, porosity, and surface area creates a harmonious interplay
that affects sound absorption properties. Achieving a resonant quality in cement-based materials heavily relies on their composition.
For instance, the selection of aggregates impacts both the density and permeability of the resulting concrete, as explained by Mehta and

Considering this composition aspect, the incorporation of lightweight aggregates presents an avenue to explore. Experts suggest

many scholars, cleverly disperse air pockets within the mixture, enhancing its fluidity while maintaining the strength of the core

4. Essential frequency ranges for analysis
Selecting the range of frequencies for analyses is of utmost importance as it significantly influences the accuracy, relevance, and
depth of insights derived from the analysis. The criteria for choosing these frequencies can vary depending on factors. The inherent
characteristics of the source being examined determine which frequencies are of interest. For example, a jet engine has different noise
and vibration patterns compared to a motor [133]. As a result, their respective frequency bands for analysis will differ. Each source,
whether man-made or natural, possesses a unique spectral fingerprint that necessitates examining specific frequencies to gain a
comprehensive understanding of its behavior.
Moreover, Human perception is a critical factor in the study of acoustics, particularly in relation to comfort, health, and safety. The
human auditory system is sensitive to a frequency range of 20 Hz to 20 kHz, making this spectrum especially important in areas such as
room acoustics and noise pollution. Understanding how humans perceive different frequencies is essential for designing environments
that are acoustically comfortable and safe, taking into account the varying impacts of sound across this broad frequency range [56,64].
However, certain frequencies within this range may hold specific importance due to their perceived loudness or potential harm to
hearing [134]. Additionally, the overall context determines the general frequency range, and specific areas of interest may prioritize
certain bands over others. For example, even though both fall under room acoustics, a recording studio might focus on frequencies for
music clarity, while a lecture hall might prioritize speech intelligibility. Therefore, choosing the frequency ranges for analysis requires
consideration of various factors, including the specific needs of the application, the nature of the source material, and how humans
perceive and interpret information.
4.1. Frequency range profiles of different transport systems
In transportation, frequency analysis is a method for understanding the realm of noise and vibrations caused by different modes of
transportation. Whether it is road vehicles or complex aircraft systems, each has its set of frequencies associated with their functioning,
which has practical implications and impacts on humans. Regarding road vehicles, such as cars and trucks, various frequencies come
into play. The majority of noise produced by these vehicles falls within the lower frequency range, starting at 20 Hz. Within this
spectrum, different components and interactions contribute to specific frequency bands. The engine, often regarded as the heart of the
vehicle, primarily emits frequencies below 100 Hz [135,136]. These frequencies correspond to its combustion cycles, mechanical
movements, and overall operations. At the higher end of the range, aerodynamic interactions start influencing the generated noise at a
higher speed, resulting in higher frequencies (more than 1 kHz). Factors like vehicle shape, design, and external components also affect
noise production, which peaks around 1 kHz. Additionally, continuous contact and friction between tires and road surfaces contribute
to this range of frequencies in terms of noise [137–139].
Railways are another mode of transportation examined when analyzing distinct frequency ranges [140]. In cities, the focus
typically lies within the 20 Hz to 2 kHz range. The sounds from trains below 500 Hz can be attributed to factors such as inconsistencies
in the tracks, imperfections in the wheels, and even the distribution of weight on the train. Moving towards higher frequencies reveals
noticeable clattering noises coming from track joints or switches [141,142]. Additionally, as demonstrated by Xinwen et al., wheel
noise primarily occurs in the high-frequency range of 1600–4000 Hz, slab noise radiates in the frequency range of 125–500 Hz, and rail
noise mostly occurs in the middle and high-frequency range of 500–4000 Hz [143].
Aircraft noise exhibits diversity in nature, with the impressive encountered during takeoff comprising a combination of various
frequency sounds, while the sharp whistle associated with jet engines tends to lean towards frequencies [144]. Upon closer exami-
nation, frequencies ranging from 50 Hz up to 10 kHz become apparent, encompassing everything from engine rotations and vibrations
in the aircraft structure to aerodynamics that come into play during different phases of flight [145,146].
It is important to emphasize that selecting these frequency ranges goes beyond engineering exercises. The perception of these
sounds plays a significant role in influencing the comfort levels of passengers or individuals residing near transportation hubs. In
addition, prolonged exposure to certain frequencies at high volumes could have negative effects on health. Some frequencies are
known to cause stress and communication difficulties, potentially leading to hearing problems [147,148]. In summary, frequency
analysis reveals that road vehicles (20 Hz–100 Hz), railways (20 Hz - 2 kHz), and aircraft (50 Hz - 10 kHz) each produce distinct sound
ranges with significant implications for human comfort and health.

5. Room acoustics
Room acoustics involves the intricate study of sound source behaviors within a confined space, encompassing the reflection, ab-
sorption, and transmission of sound toward boundaries [154]. The room acoustics approach makes certain assumptions regarding the
sound field propagation in a room. Firstly, it considers a sound field consisting of direct and diffuse sound, using the sound absorption
coefficient as an indicator [155]. Secondly, it accounts for sound rays striking hard walls and being reflected in complex ways that do
not strictly follow the laws of optical reflection. The reflection is influenced by factors such as the surface roughness and the angle of
incidence [30]. Thirdly, it represents sound using wave theory, employing analytical solutions of the wave equation through numerical
approximation methods such as Finite Element Method (FEM). In addition to FEM, the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method
is also a viable approach for wave acoustic simulation. Both methods have their unique advantages and applications in room acoustics.
These methods are employed to obtain suitable acoustic parameters, contributing to the creation of a comfortable acoustic environ-
ment within the room.
Acoustic comfort, a crucial aspect of Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) criteria [31], is a prominent concern within the realm of
room acoustics. This issue arises from the volume of people utilizing a space over a period [156] and directly influences human
psychological well-being [157]. Research in public spaces, such as hospitals, has highlighted dissatisfaction among occupants
regarding sound privacy and noise exposure [31]. Achieving satisfaction requires effective acoustic treatment in the room. For optimal
acoustic comfort, two factors should be considered: (1) controlling outdoor sound with sound insulation and (2) controlling indoor
sound with reverberation time and sound absorption [158]. Acousticians need to examine different ranges of frequency due to the
different purposes of uses, and different SAC values of materials.
Previous research in multipurpose halls involved acoustic treatment for curtains, walls, and floors, along with the addition of
absorption materials [159]. However, historical and ancient structures, like church buildings, may pose challenges for renovation,
leaving them categorized as uncomfortable due to non-compliance with standards [160]. In addition to the sound absorption coef-
ficient, the Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC) also can be used to assess how well sound waves reach a material and are absorbed
rather than reflected into the room. The NRC value falls between 0 and 1, indicating total reflection and absorption, respectively.
Although a high NRC signifies effective overall sound absorption, it does not offer insights into the performance of the material at
either low or high frequencies. Consequently, if a room is experiencing problems with sounds within these frequency ranges, a material
possessing a high NRC may not necessarily provide an effective solution. Therefore, while materials with a high NRC can help reduce
overall noise levels, it also may not necessarily improve the quality of the sound within the room, rather it can make the room sound
“dead” or non-reverberant. While this might be desirable in some situations (like in a recording studio), it can also negatively impact
interpersonal communication and the perception of speech at normal volumes.
To address this, standards have been established for each room type based on function, aiming to achieve acoustic comfort.
Standards such as ISO 3382–1:209 guide acoustic treatment to achieve standard parameters in a room, including reverberation time
(T30), Clarity (C80), Definition (D50), and Strength (G) are crucial for room acoustics [151]. These parameters help in evaluating the
acoustic quality of a room:
• Reverberation time (T30): The amount of time needed for the sound pressure to decay by 30 dB.
• Clarity (C80): Measures the clarity of sound, particularly useful for speech intelligibility and music.
• Definition (D50): Indicates the percentage of early-arriving sound energy relative to the total sound energy.
• Strength (G): Measures the amplification or attenuation of sound within the room. These parameters are integral to the design
method discussed in Chapter 5.2 and will be referred to throughout the section.
ANSI/ASA S12.60 gives guidance on measurement methods and acoustic evaluation for buildings, with a focus on noise, sound
isolation, and speech intelligibility, especially for core-learning space [161]. Additionally, ISO 717-1 provides a method for calculating
a single-number rating for sound insulation from data measured as a function of frequency [162]. It is not used for direct measurement
but rather for interpreting measured data.
To fulfill these requirements, the function of the room must be carefully considered, especially regarding the selection of surface
materials for walls, floors, and ceilings. Different room applications, such as music studios, concert halls, and theaters, necessitate the
thoughtful installation of absorption materials. Additionally, factors such as room geometry, partitions, furniture, and background
noise all play significant roles in shaping the acoustic quality of the space.

5.1. Materials used
As mentioned earlier, when sound interacts with surfaces in a room, it undergoes absorption, reflection, and transmission. The
nature of this surface, composed of various materials and shapes, significantly influences human perception of sound and the acoustic
comfort of the room. Each material possesses a distinct absorption coefficient, a factor that directly impacts the propagation of sound
within the room. The ability of a material to absorb sound is directly proportional to its absorption coefficient, measured on a scale
from 0 to 1, where higher values indicate better sound absorption. In comparison, hard surfaces like walls and tiles absorb much less
sound energy than soft, porous objects such as humans, carpets, and furniture [154]. When a sound wave encounters these absorbers,
the air within their connected pores vibrates. However, due to the flow resistance of the material restricting the movement of air
particles, some of the sound energy is dissipated as heat [154].
In designing room acoustics, diverse materials are selected for each surface. For instance, a multifunction hall study aimed to
enhance acoustic comfort by opting for a heavy curtain with a higher sound absorption coefficient, employing durable parquet on the
concrete floor, and the stage floor made of solid wood with a 500 mm air gap partially filled with absorbing material. Varied single and
double board constructions with different depths were used for the side walls to manage low-frequency absorption [163]. Another
study, focused on improving acoustic comfort on a university campus, included noise barrier such as an insulation barrier and a
double-skin facade to reduce classroom noise [158]. In addition, the use of padded chair for the audience and lightweight curtains to
cover the window had a significant impact due to their substantial sound absorption properties [159,164]. Furthermore, a plasterboard
lining system composed of a viscoelastic multilayer was proposed in a previous study as an absorbing material. The sound reduction
index demonstrated superior performance in sound insulation, reducing noise by up to 53 dB in frequency 2500 Hz, and achieving a
sound absorption coefficient exceeding 0.5 across all frequencies [165].
5.2. Design method
Room acoustics encompass two primary design approaches: passive and active. Passive design involves adjusting surface materials
such as walls, floor, and ceiling to meet acoustics standards which are mentioned in ISO 3382-1 and discussed in detail in section 5
introduction, this includes reverberation time, clarity, definition, and strength. On the other hand, active design entails incorporating a
sound reinforcement system within the room, promoting uniform sound distribution.
Before implementing any acoustic design in a room, it is crucial to assess the quality of the audience experience. This involves
measuring the room’s acoustic properties, typically using an omnidirectional sound source, and positioning the sound receiver
following its intended function. Reverberation time, a parameter introduced by Sabine in Equation (11) is commonly employed as an
indicator to achieve the desired quality in room acoustics [166].

6.3. Acoustic simulation
6.3.1. Type of simulation
The method of simulating sound varies depending on the object. In-room acoustics, using auralization is one of the implementations
for acoustic simulation, employing ray tracing for creating audible sound files from numerical (simulated, measured, or synthesized)
data of the room [32]. Auralization is analogous to visualization but for sound. Auralization involves simulating how sound propagates
within a given space and then converting those simulations into audio that can be listened to, allowing users to experience how a space
would sound. Similar to the way light waves travel across the room, sound waves and energy follow a similar principle [30]. Acoustic
environment simulations are widely used in diverse settings such as classrooms, performance spaces, open-plan offices, and concert
halls. In the simulation, a sound source generates an impulse, and the acoustics of the room are simulated. Particles are launched
simultaneously but in different directions to simulate this process. Each ray produces a specific amount of energy, travels at the speed
of sound, and occasionally collides with the room’s boundaries. Upon hitting a wall, the ray reflects, strikes another wall, and un-
dergoes a reduction in energy due to wall absorption [32]. Specialized acoustics software designed for room acoustics has employed
this method.
An alternative method for acoustic simulation involves the utilization of a wave-based approach, implemented through a numerical
wave equation method. This method is employed to simulate the acoustic characteristics of specific materials, allowing for the
derivation of various acoustic effects, including diffraction, radiation, transmission, scattering, and absorption [147]. Simulations in
this method are conducted in the frequency domain using Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD), Boundary Element Methods (BEM),
and Finite Element Methods (FEM) [32]. These simulations can be performed using advanced multiphysics software tools that support
comprehensive acoustic modeling capabilities.
Furthermore, acoustic simulations for sound reinforcement systems and urban environments are available for investigating
environmental soundscapes. A sound reinforcement system, commonly known with speaker and microphone, can be simulated
through Multiphysics software. In this case, not only acoustics but also the structure of the object is important. Software such as
COMSOL allows for simulation using acoustic-structure interaction module. In this scenario, the pressure exerted by the fluid generates
a load on the solid region, while the acceleration of the structure impacts the fluid region as an ordinary acceleration across the
boundary separating the fluid and solid domains [147].
Apart from simulations on materials and surfaces, acoustic simulations can also be conducted in environmental contexts, such as
outdoor noise simulations and soundscape simulations. Acoustic simulations in outdoor environments typically focus on predicting
and analyzing noise levels and their propagation, with the aim of noise classification and mitigation.
On the other hand, soundscape simulations approach the audio environment, encompassing all surrounding sounds to understand
and enhance the overall auditory experience. Soundscape studies often focus on urban environments, analyzing the interplay of
various sounds such as traffic, conversations, footsteps, and other ambient noises. The goal is not only to mitigate unwanted noise but
also to enhance positive acoustic elements, contributing to the overall quality of life. Presently, numerous soundscape studies
concentrate on sounds within urban environments. Professionals are actively working on establishing discussion tools for urban
soundscapes using advanced acoustic modeling platforms [182]. The development of soundscape software, which aims to provide a
comprehensive auditory experience by integrating human perception and environmental sounds, is currently the subject of extensive
research.
In addition to acoustics simulation, the auralization method is also applied. This method can be employed using a dummy head
model or directly with human subjects. In this approach, participants are exposed to sounds resulting from the convolution of a room’s
impulse response and a specific sound source, such as speech or music. The convolution process creates an auditory experience that
mimics the natural occurrence of sounds within the simulated room. The auralization method is utilized to provide participants with an

With ongoing advancement in the construction and architectural industries, there is a growing emphasis on discovering materials
that combine functionality with sustainability [192]. Cementitious compounds have gained recognition for their reliability and
adaptability [128]. This section explores the potential of materials in applications, marking an emerging area of interest. However, like

However, despite the use of various simulation tools in the field of acoustics, numerous research has also demonstrated that the
simulations in acoustic studies are not 100 % accurate and discrepancies can occur when compared with experimental results. Berardi
et al. [193] address the issue of reliability in simulating the acoustic performance compared to the measurement of acoustic parameters
in the building, the error between these methods was found in the octave band of 4 kHz for the acoustic parameter based on ISO 3382-1
[151].
Branda˜o et al. [194] and Brinkmann et al. [195] discuss the limited accuracy of the modeling using room acoustics simulation. In
that case, diffraction and scattering were shown to introduce an error, especially for the low-frequency range. It also found that among

parameters. Some factors, such as the ideal settings in the software used for modeling and the actual conditions in the measurements,
contribute to this discrepancy. Desmond et al. [196] compared the predicted model and experiment of the acoustics properties of
biodegradables and found the difference in the peak value of the sound absorption coefficient. The use of simulation is nevertheless
acceptable despite not being completely accurate because it offers efficient options to understand the effect of different types of
materials and geometry of structures on acoustic properties.
In the construction industry, cementitious materials, traditionally valued for their durability and strength [113], necessitate

7.1. Cost
Cost considerations are crucial in assessing the economic feasibility of materials, particularly in industries with tight budgets where
evaluation of cost-benefit analysis is essential. The discourse surrounding materials engineered for sound absorption is grounded in
empirical evidence, with numerous studies quantifying their impacts [201]. For instance, conventional cementitious materials
inherently lack sound-absorbing properties, necessitating significant alterations to impart such characteristics. Fediuk et al. quanti-
tatively assessed that these modifications, ranging from the integration of additives to alterations in manufacturing processes, can
result in a cost increase or decrease of approximately 10–30 %, depending on the additive used [68]. One notable modification is the
development of pervious concrete, offering superior sound absorption due to its intrinsic porosity, capable of attenuating sound waves
by as much as 20–35 % more effectively than standard concrete [68]. Nonetheless, the production of such aerated materials typically
requires additional steps, such as the incorporation of chemical agents, which can increase the costs based on the dosage and the agent
used compared to traditional concrete.
Therefore, while the utilization of modified materials for absorption holds potential in acoustic engineering, industry professionals
should carefully consider financial challenges. Adopters and stakeholders need to balance these costs against the advantages of
durability and potential energy savings or other efficiencies the material may offer. Making informed decisions about the feasibility of
using these materials in various applications requires a comprehensive understanding of the complex economic factors involved [128].
In summary, the improvement of cementitious materials for sound absorption can lead to cost increases of 10–30 %, despite offering
20–35 % better sound attenuation than conventional concrete.
7.2. Durability
The long-term performance and sustainability of construction materials fundamentally rely on their durability. Cementitious
materials, traditionally valued for their robustness in construction projects, present a unique challenge when modified to enhance
sound absorption properties, as these alterations may inadvertently compromise their longevity [202–204]. For example, increasing
the porosity of cementitious materials to enhance absorption capabilities can intensify their vulnerability to weathering. Statistical
data indicate that in regions with pronounced seasonal temperature shifts or frequent freeze-thaw cycles, porous materials may
experience a reduction in durability of up to 25 % due to accelerated micro-crack formation, compared to non-modified counterparts
[205]. This environmental degradation can necessitate premature repair or replacement, potentially increasing lifecycle costs by an
amount equivalent to the effect of freeze and thaw over a standard 50-year period [206].
Regarding physical robustness, porous materials exhibit a lower density, and studies indicate that their compressive strength can be
reduced by 10–30 % compared to non-porous varieties [167,207]. In areas of high traffic or mechanical interaction, such as industrial
zones, transportation hubs, or public spaces, the resilience of these modified materials to impacts is a significant consideration. Cu-
mulative damage from repeated physical contact could lead to higher structural failure rates compared to traditional materials [23,44,
115,208].
Beyond physical and environmental challenges, cementitious materials with increased porosity may also encounter biological
hazards. In conditions favorable to mold and mildew growth, such as high humidity or poor ventilation, the risk of bio-growth on
porous surfaces significantly increases [209]. This biological activity not only deteriorate the material’s structure and appearance but
also pose health hazards, impacting indoor air quality [210–212]. Furthermore, in regions with high pollution levels, chemical
degradation from factors like road salt or acid rain can further decrease in the material’s sound absorption efficiency and structural
integrity by an additional 10–20 % [212–214].
In conclusion, while the primary aim of modifying cementitious materials is to enhance their sound-absorbing capabilities, these
changes can introduce durability-related challenges that require careful evaluation. Industry professionals and researchers need to
devise strategies that address these potential downsides. This may involve an increase in initial material costs by 5–15 % to incorporate
protective coatings or design alterations that fortify the material against such vulnerabilities, thereby ensuring the material’s long-term
efficacy and cost-efficiency [128]. It should be noted that enhancing cementitious materials for sound absorption can reduce their
durability, with porous materials facing up to 25 % reduced longevity and 10–30 % decrease in compressive strength. Implementing
additional protective measures to counteract these effects may increase initial costs by 5–15 %. In summary, modifying cementitious
materials for sound absorption can lead to a reduction in their durability, with porous materials experiencing up to 25–30 % less
longevity and a 10–30 % decrease in compressive strength. Addressing these issues with protective measures and design alterations
could increase initial costs by 5–15 % but is necessary to ensure long-term efficacy and cost-efficiency.
7.3. Potential negative environmental impacts
Cement-based materials constitute a fundamental element in contemporary construction and infrastructure. However, their pro-
duction and utilization raise environmental concerns that necessitate a comprehensive quantitative assessment. For instance, the

In terms of greenhouse gas emissions, the cement industry stands out as one of the most energy-intensive sectors, contributing to

indicate that approximately 0.9 tons of CO2 are released into the atmosphere for every tone of cement production [218,219].
Moreover, the modification of cementitious materials to improve their properties may necessitate the incorporation of specialized
additives, potentially leading to a 10–20 % increase in production waste [220]. If these additives or their by-products are not managed
sustainably, this could lead to a proportional increase in landfill contributions. Consequently, non-biodegradable waste may release
harmful chemicals into the soil and groundwater systems, posing potential toxic effects that could persist for decades [220,221].
Water usage in cement production is another environmental factor, with the industry consuming 9 % or more of global industrial
water withdrawals annually, which is approximately 1.7 % of total global water withdrawal [222,223]. Modifying cement to enhance
properties can inadvertently increase this figure by 5–10 %, exacerbating water scarcity challenges. The intensified water consumption
can deplete local water sources, adversely impact wetland ecosystems, and lead to a reduction in biodiversity in aquatic systems by up
to 3–5% [223,224].
The evidence highlights a substantial environmental footprint associated with cement production, necessitating comprehensive
measures to mitigate impacts. This includes the need for innovations in production processes that could potentially reduce CO2
emissions by up to 20–25 % [225], advancements in waste management to minimize landfill contributions, and improved water
conservation techniques that could lower water usage by as much as 10–15 % in the cement industry. These measures are not only
environmentally critical but also increasingly mandated by regulatory frameworks and sustainable practice standards [226]. In
summary, the cement industry contributes 7–8% to global CO2 emissions, with enhanced acoustic processing potentially increasing
emissions and production waste. Furthermore, it consumes over 9 % of industrial water withdrawals, highlighting the need for more
sustainable production and resource management practices.
7.4. Summary
Cementitious materials are increasingly recognized for their potential as valuable assets in the field of sound absorption across
various applications [227]. Their unique composition, structure, and modifications make them appealing solutions to address acoustic
challenges [228]. However, the complexities surrounding their integration into spaces and applications become apparent, as sum-
marized in this review paper. Considering this aspect, it is crucial not to overlook the cost implications of these materials. While
understanding the initial production and establishment of cementitious materials, incorporating sound absorption enhancements can
introduce additional expenses [128]. These costs include research and development, sourcing additives, and potentially requiring
installation techniques. Industry professionals should consider the financial investment and long-term maintenance costs that can
impact overall ownership expenses.
Durability is another concern, as the modifications that enhance sound absorption materials could unintentionally compromise
their longevity [192]. Whether it is an increased susceptibility to wear and tear, vulnerability to various factors, or reduced structural
integrity due to heightened porosity these challenges cannot be brushed aside. For any material to gain acceptance it must demonstrate
resilience over time in demanding or variable conditions. Moreover, the environmental implications add another layer of complexity.
In a world increasingly moving towards solutions, there is a growing focus on scrutinizing the impact of any material or solution [229].
The cement industry has an environmental footprint and increased production, and modification of cementitious materials could
worsen this impact. Therefore, considering sourcing, production methods, and proper disposal in this context becomes crucial.
Amid these challenges, there is a growing focus on sustainable practices within the industry, highlighted by advances in supple-
mentary cementitious materials such as fly ash, slag, and innovative substances including calcined clays and recycled glass [51,230].
These materials reduce the negative effects of cement in construction and demolition by lowering CO2 emissions and enhancing
durability and performance. Technologies such as carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) and the development of low-carbon
cement are also pivotal in advancing sustainability. Furthermore, recycling and reusing materials from construction and demolition
contribute significantly to resource conservation [192].
Considering these multifaceted challenges, it is evident that while cementitious materials show promise, their widespread adoption
is not straightforward. This highlights the need for research and development, fostering efforts among material scientists, acousticians,
environmentalists, and industry stakeholders. These collective endeavors can drive innovations that optimize the properties of
cementitious materials, ensuring they are cost-effective, durable, and environmentally sustainable. Ultimately, cementitious materials
have the potential for absorption applications. However, realizing this potential requires an approach to address inherent challenges
and ensure that the solutions developed are both feasible and beneficial in the long run. In summary, cementitious materials hold the
potential in sound absorption but face challenges such as increased production costs, durability concerns, and environmental impact.
Collaborative efforts among various experts are essential to optimize these materials for cost-effectiveness, longevity, and sustain-
ability, ensuring their practicality in absorption applications.

8. Conclusion
The significance and capabilities of cementitious materials in sound absorption continue to grow, playing a pivotal role in the ever-
evolving field of acoustics. This review provides a historical perspective on how sound management has influenced human experi-
ences, ranging from the design of ancient theaters to the architecture of contemporary urban environments. Emphasizing the esca-
lating challenge of noise pollution, disrupting the tranquility of spaces and adversely affecting public health and psychological well-
being, the review highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the materials and methodologies to effectively mitigate noise.
Considering the comprehensive review conducted in this study, the following conclusions have been drawn:
1. The selection of the appropriate method for measuring sound absorption, whether it involves the reverberation chamber,
impedance tube, or in-situ surface impedance, depends on the material characteristics and the specific context of use. Adhering to
standards such as ASTM C423-17 and ISO 10534, each method has its trade-offs, including the large sample requirement of the
reverberation chamber, the size limitations of impedance tube, and the environmental sensitivity of the in-situ method. Ultimately,
a customized approach, potentially integrating multiple techniques and utilizing metrics such as NRC, SAA, or SAAR, is crucial for
an accurate evaluation of a material’s sound absorption properties.
2. The modification of concrete with various materials, such as crumb rubber, bottom ash, and lightweight aggregates, significantly
enhances its sound absorption properties. Rubberized concrete, with a 30 % crumb rubber content, exhibits optimal absorption,
while bottom ash enhances acoustic performance due to its porosity. Additionally, concrete with up to 40 % lightweight Ceno-
sphere demonstrates improved sound absorption. These innovative modifications not only improve the acoustic properties of
concrete but also contribute to the development of more sustainable and versatile construction materials.
3. The acoustic performance of construction materials relies on finding a balance between density, porosity, and surface area. High-
density materials exhibit durability but are less efficient in sound absorption, whereas porosity and large surface areas with
complex geometries enhance absorption. Achieving optimization in these aspects necessitates careful consideration of lightweight
aggregates, pore-forming agents, and water-to-cement ratios to ensure both structural integrity and effective sound absorption.
4. Frequency analysis is crucial across diverse domains: road vehicles emit noise between 20 Hz and 100 Hz, railways range from 20
Hz to 2 kHz, and aircraft noise spans 50 Hz to 10 kHz, impacting human comfort and health. Room acoustics focus from 50 Hz to 10
kHz, with speech frequencies between 50 Hz and 4 kHz (fundamental tone from 50 Hz to 350 Hz) and music in concert halls
extending from 20 Hz to 12–16 kHz. This emphasizes the importance of targeted specific frequency ranges in sound environments.
5. Various theoretical models in acoustics, ranging from the straightforward Delany-Bazley-Miki to the comprehensive Johnson-
Champoux-Allard-Lafarge, demonstrate the trade-off between simplicity and accuracy in analyzing sound absorption in porous
materials. The selection of a model depends on the balance between the availability of material parameters and the desired pre-
cision in acoustic analysis, highlighting the complexity and diversity of approaches in this field.
6. Acoustic simulation methods exhibit considerable variation, as demonstrated by room acoustic simulations in ODEON and CATT-
Acoustics, which reveal up to a 20 % difference in reverberation time attributable to modeling approaches. In material studies,
COMSOL and ANSYS Acoustics exhibit a 6.6 % discrepancy between simulation and experimental results, highlighting the precision
and diversity of acoustic simulation applications.
7. While cementitious materials hold promise for sound absorption, they present challenges such as increased costs (10–30 %),
reduced durability (up to 25–30 % less longevity, 10–30 % lower strength), and significant environmental impact, including high
CO2 emissions (7–8% of global emissions) and increased water usage. Addressing these issues necessitates a balanced approach and
collaborative research to optimize their utilization in a cost-effective, durable, and sustainable manner.
The considerable potential of modified cementitious materials in sound absorbing is evident. However, as in any continuously
evolving field, researchers face challenges. This review highlights the significance of adopting an approach that combines the expertise
of acoustic scientists and material engineers, considering environmental factors to advance sound management in the future. In the
face of the increasing complexity of modern urban life, it becomes crucial to seek solutions that are not only effective but also sus-
tainable and practical.
